newsitem.title: CANADA: Thousands flee as Red River swallows Manitoba town.
newsitem.headline: Thousands flee as Red River swallows Manitoba town.

text.p: Thousands of residents of Manitoba's largest city scrambled for higher ground on Tuesday because of fear of Red River flooding like as it did towns in Minnesota, North Dakota and in the southern part of the province.
Soldiers rescued 37 people from Ste. Agathe, a town of 477 people 20 miles (32 km) south of Winnipeg, as a six-foot (two metres) wall of water submerged the town early Tuesday.

About 3,000 rural Manitobans and 8,000 Winnipeggers were ordered to out of their homes on Tuesday ahead of the rising Red River, bringing the total number of Canadian flood evacuees to 28,000. About 50,000 people from Grand Forks, North Dakota, remained homeless after the river's crest there 10 days ago.

Winnipeggers' fears focused on a nearly complete but quickly built 25-mile (40 km) earthen dike along the city's southwest flank and the ability of a massive Floodway ditch on the southeast to part the flood waters of the rising "Red Sea."

"If you look at what happened in Grand Forks I think there's the potential for the same kind of disaster here. Even with the Floodway it's all still a very big unknown," Sheldon Bartel said as he and his wife prepared to abandon their home.
South Winnipeg on Tuesday was teeming with trucks, armoured personnel carriers and emergency vehicles that carried people and property out of the city's most vulnerable district.
"It feels weird being part of history instead of just listening to the stories of the 1950 flood and now we're going to be part of the '97 flood," Peggy Bartel added.

The Floodway was built in 1968 to divert high Red River waters around the limits of this city of 650,000. The ditch was built after a flood in 1950 forced the evacuation of 100,000 residents. Th current flood could cover twice the area flooded in 1950 to as much as 800 square miles (2,072 sq km).

"We are trying to manage the unknown. As the mayor of this city I'm sure glad I'm here with these people right about now," Winnipeg Mayor Susan Thompson said choking back tears at a briefing with municipal engineers.

The usually tame Red River swelled to 22 times its normal flow this month as record-breaking winter snows melted. The flood could be the worst in Manitoba since 1852 and it evoked memories of more recent devastation.
"The last time I was evacuated was in 1950. The flood waters were as high then as they already are now," Mike Tataryn said as he emptied his south Winnipeg home.
Laura Rance prepared to evacuate after she was ordered to leaver her Sanford area home southwest of Winnipeg by Tuesday night along with 3,000 other rural residents.
"People are really anxious. We weren't supposed to get water here so there's a sense of injustice. This took people by surprise," Rance said.
Winnipeg crews began on Monday to reinforce a highway surrounding the city as a last line of defence for people living in the city's southwest.
